claim: The data covers 1,656 conversations, each with two rows of ratings in the people table (3,312 rows), from 1,456 distinct participants.
754 of the 1,456 participants appear in more than one conversation, and 3 appear in eight.
Among the 3,257 people with all four ratings, average mood rose from 6.1 before the call to 6.16 at the beginning, 6.93 in the middle and 7.38 at the end.
69.2% of people felt better at the end of the conversation than before it, 20.5% felt the same and 10.3% felt worse.
Energy (arousal) also rose: from an average of 5.32 before the call to 6.41 after it.
People said they liked their partner 6.00 on average but guessed their partner liked them only 5.35.
Compared with what the partner actually reported, 54.9% of people underestimated how much their partner liked them, 26.8% guessed exactly and 18.3% overestimated (3,206 people with both ratings).
43% of people gave their partner a liking score of 7, but only 17% guessed their partner gave them a 7.
A person's guess of how much the partner liked them correlates 0.69 with how much they liked the partner, but only 0.19 with how much the partner actually liked them.
The two partners' ratings of how enjoyable the conversation was correlate only 0.17.
The same gap shows for traits: pair averages rate the partner 7.68 for intelligence but guess the partner rated them 7.06; for kindness 7.98 against 7.43.
In pair averages, rated liking of the partner exceeded the guessed liking in 73.4% of conversations and fell below it in 5.3%; for intelligence the figures are 67.6% and 13.4%.
People rated their own turns as longer than their partner's: 5.40 against 5.03 on average across pairs, with the own-turn rating higher in 51.47% of conversations and lower in 23.89%.

claim: Enjoyment climbs steeply with a person's shared-reality score: 5.25 for scores of 3 or below, 6.71 for 3-4, 7.46 for 4-5, 7.98 for 5-6 and 8.55 above 6.
A person's shared-reality score correlates 0.58 with how enjoyable they found the conversation and 0.53 with how much they liked their partner.
Demographic mismatch barely moves enjoyment: pairs of different sex average 7.44 against 7.38 for same sex, different race 7.34 against 7.46, and different education 7.5 against 7.3.
Political distance has a modest effect: pairs with the same political score average 7.48 enjoyment, against 7.15 for a gap of 4 (115 pairs) and 7.07 for a gap of 5 (23 pairs).
When the two partners' shared-reality scores differ by 4 points, pairs average 6.44 enjoyment against 7.52 when they match (31 and 454 pairs).
